gameplay_summary: Overhead action-adventure: as Link, explore Hyrule's overworld and dungeons, collecting the eight fragments of the Triforce of Wisdom and items like heart containers and rings, to rescue Princess Zelda from Ganon.
dossier: Nintendo's 1994 cartridge release of The Hyrule Fantasy: Zelda no Densetsu, first released on the Disk System in 1986 as its launch title and the start of the Zelda series, designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka. Link explores Hyrule from a flip-screen overhead view, starting with only a small shield until an old man in a cave gives him a sword. He seeks the eight fragments of the Triforce of Wisdom to rescue Princess Zelda from Ganon. Heart containers extend his life meter, and rings reduce damage. At full health his sword fires a beam. The cartridge lacks the Disk System's extra sound channel, so as on the western cartridge, the title music and fonts changed.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Exploration is visual, but old men's hints are in Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as The Legend of Zelda (1987).
japanese_version_notes: A 1994 cartridge re-release of the 1986 Disk System original, with the same music and font changes as the western cartridge.

gameplay_summary: Bomb-matching puzzle: as Toad, rearrange the monsters and bombs that a sprite drops into the forest, lining up monsters with same-coloured bombs to clear them all, in Round Game, Time Race or two-player versus.
dossier: Nintendo's last Famicom release in Japan, developed by Nintendo R&D1 and Intelligent Systems. In North America it was the final licensed NES game and the only one with an ESRB rating. Wario has taken over the Peaceful Woods, and Toad sets out to drive him out. Monsters and bombs fall from above, and you can speed their fall but not move or rotate them. Instead, Toad rearranges the landed pieces to line up monsters with same-coloured bombs. Modes are the one-player Round Game and Time Race, two-player versus, and a lesson mode. There's no score, and the battery saves names, progress and records.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — A visual puzzle; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Wario's Woods (North America 1994).

gameplay_summary: Compilation of the first two Final Fantasy games on one cartridge, chosen from the title screen with separate saves.
dossier: Square's last Famicom release, a tie-in with the New Famicom that puts Final Fantasy (FC-0289) and Final Fantasy II (FC-0427) on one cartridge. FamiWiki notes it was the last RPG of all released for the Famicom. Unlike Super Famicom remakes of the same era, it simply combines the two original games with almost no changes. You pick either from its logo on the title screen, and their save data is fully separate. The logo uses the font from Final Fantasy IV onward, the box shows super-deformed art in the style of IV and V, and a special strategy guide was included. In the first game, the Beholder and Death Beholder monsters have new graphics.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Two Japanese-language RPGs.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Compilation cartridge with a bundled strategy guide; Beholder graphics changed in FF I.

gameplay_summary: Third Pachi-Slot Adventure slot game; the sources give no further detail.
dossier: The third Pachi-Slot Adventure, developed by Aisystem Tokyo and released on 13 May 1994. FamiWiki says it was the last gambling game on the Famicom. FamiWiki credits C Dream as publisher, while the census lists Coconuts Japan. gameplay_summary: J.League soccer: lead your chosen club to the championship in exhibition, season, playoff or practice modes, for one or two players.
dossier: The only Famicom game published by Electronic Arts (as EA Victor), developed by Graphic Research and based on a Game Boy version released two months earlier. FamiWiki says it was the last sports game on the Famicom. The goal is to win the J.League title and make your club Japan's best, with exhibition, season, playoff and practice modes. FamiWiki notes the Game Boy version's EA splash screen graphics are left unused in the Famicom cartridge, and lists both Japanese and English text.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Soccer is visual; menus mix Japanese and English.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Open-map Adventure Island: as Takahashi Meijin, explore a connected scrolling world rather than separate stages, using items like boomerangs, spears and a water gun to solve puzzles and rescue his five kidnapped dinosaur friends.
dossier: Hudson's last Takahashi Meijin no Bouken Jima, and the final officially licensed Famicom game. Hudson's sales team reckoned that, with no one else still developing for the Famicom, a new release could sell tens of thousands, and chose Adventure Island for its quick development and simple rights. A mysterious being kidnaps Takahashi Meijin's five dinosaur companions, and he sets out to rescue them. Instead of separate stages, a complex scrolling map links everything. He climbs trees and enters doors, and uses items as weapons, like boomerangs and spears, or to solve puzzles, like the water gun. It was pitched at beginners and was well made, but the generational shift made it a commercial failure, Hudson's lowest-selling Famicom game.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Exploration is visual, but puzzle hints are Japanese.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
